cardiac-output.short: The volume of blood the heart pumps per minute: heart rate × stroke volume, in L·min⁻¹. About 5 L·min⁻¹ at rest, several times more at maximal exercise.

stroke-volume.short: The volume of blood one ventricle pushes out in one beat, in mL. About 70 mL at rest in an untrained adult.

end-diastolic-volume.short: The volume of blood in a ventricle when it has finished filling, just before it contracts. It is the usual measure of preload.

ejection-fraction.short: The share of the filled ventricle's blood pushed out in one beat: stroke volume ÷ end-diastolic volume. About 55–70% at rest.

preload.short: How much the ventricle is stretched by filling before it contracts, set by venous return and filling time. More preload, bigger stroke volume.

contractility.short: The strength of the heart muscle's contraction at a given filling. Sympathetic nerves and adrenaline raise it, emptying the ventricle more.

afterload.short: The pressure the ventricle must overcome to push blood out, mainly the arterial pressure behind the aortic valve. More afterload, smaller stroke volume.

frank-starling.short: Within limits, the more the ventricle is stretched by filling, the harder it contracts: more blood in, more blood out.

hrmax.short: The highest heart rate reached in an all-out effort. It falls with age and is best measured, since age formulas typically miss by about 11 beats·min⁻¹.

intrinsic-heart-rate.short: The rate the sinoatrial node fires at when both autonomic branches are blocked by drugs: the heart's own pace without nervous input.

sinus-bradycardia.short: A resting heart rate below about 60 beats·min⁻¹ with normal pacing from the sinoatrial node. Common and usually harmless in endurance athletes.

vasodilation.short: Widening of a blood vessel as the smooth muscle in its wall relaxes. It lowers resistance, so more blood flows at the same pressure. Opposite: vasoconstriction.

functional-sympatholysis.short: The blunting of sympathetic vasoconstriction inside contracting muscle by local signals, so active muscle keeps its blood flow while other beds clamp down.

muscle-pump.short: Contracting muscles squeeze the veins inside them; with one-way valves, this pushes blood towards the heart and keeps venous pressure in the working limb low.

mean-arterial-pressure.short: The average pressure in the arteries over a heartbeat, which drives blood into the tissues. Roughly diastolic + one third of the pulse pressure.

pulse-pressure.short: Systolic minus diastolic blood pressure, e.g. 120 − 80 = 40 mmHg. It widens in endurance exercise as systolic rises and diastolic holds.

exercise-pressor-reflex.short: A reflex from active muscle: sensory nerves that detect stretch, pressure and the chemical by-products of work raise sympathetic activity, heart rate and blood pressure.

baroreflex.short: Pressure sensors in the aorta and carotid arteries adjust heart rate and vessel tone to hold blood pressure near a set point. In exercise the set point moves up.

valsalva.short: Breathing out hard against a closed throat, as when straining on a heavy lift. Pressure in the chest rises and adds to arterial pressure.

cardiovascular-drift.short: The slow rise in heart rate and fall in stroke volume during prolonged exercise at a constant power or pace, starting after about 10 minutes.
